description: Data science freaks, nature lovers, excited about birds and equality.
summary:
Know Your Field is a web app that gives farmers in Wielkopolska, one of Poland’s driest farming regions, simple soil-water guidance for each of their fields. On a satellite map, each field is coloured by its water status on a chosen date. Clicking a field shows a plain-language verdict (“slightly dry – keep an eye on it”) and the reasons behind it.
The app combines NASA data (POWER/MERRA-2, SMAP, SRTM) with ERA5-Land weather and 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery. It compares soil moisture with what is normal for that time of year and estimates each field’s 30-day water balance from rainfall and crop water use. Two machine-learning models add to this: one flags likely crop water stress, the other highlights unusual months and explains what made them unusual.
Most climate and soil data describe whole regions, while drought hits individual fields. Know Your Field turns open satellite data into practical, field-level hints that support, but do not replace, the farmer’s own judgement.
details:
What it does

Know Your Field answers one practical question: how is the water situation on my field, and should I go and check it?

A satellite map of Wielkopolska shows each monitored field (five pilot fields, 48–120 ha) coloured green (normal), yellow (slightly dry), red (clearly dry) or blue (very wet). Clicking a field opens a panel with:

  • A plain-language verdict with reasons, for example: “Soil is drier than usual for this time of year (18th percentile)”, “Over the last 30 days the field lacked about 52 mm of water”, “Image from 12 Jul: leaf water lower than expected – possible stress”. If the soil is likely frozen, the panel says so and warns that readings are less reliable.
  • Three key numbers: soil moisture compared with normal (0–100), the 30-day water balance in mm, and the date of the latest clear satellite image.
  • Four tabs:
    1. Soil water: this year’s soil moisture against the typical range for each time of year (2020–2025).
    2. Crops: green cover (NDVI) and leaf water (NDMI) from Sentinel-2, with possible water-stress events marked.
    3. Rainfall: monthly rainfall against the average of other years.
    4. Unusual months: how unusual each month was on this field, with short explanations such as “rainfall ↓, leaf water ↓, air dryness ↑”.

A date picker lets users go back to any day since 2020, for example a past dry spell, to see what the panel would have shown.

How it works

A Python pipeline downloads open data, cleans it and builds a daily table for each field:

  1. Weather and water use. Daily ERA5-Land weather (Copernicus) feeds an FAO-56 Penman–Monteith calculation of reference evapotranspiration (ET0). Sentinel-2 NDVI is converted into a crop coefficient, which gives the crop’s actual water use. Rainfall minus that use, summed over 30 days, gives a water balance for this field. Two neighbouring fields with different crops get different results.
  2. “Normal for this time of year.” Soil moisture from NASA POWER / MERRA-2 is ranked against the same ±15-day window in every year from 2020 to 2025. “Dry” therefore means dry for this place and this season, so no local soil calibration is needed.
  3. Satellite quality control. 1,184 Sentinel-2 scenes were screened for cloud, snow and one-off drops caused by cloud shadows. The 1,094 scenes that passed were interpolated into daily series; gaps longer than 30 days were left empty.
  4. Crop water-stress model. A gradient-boosting model predicts leaf water (NDMI) on each satellite overpass from the field’s previous state, the weather since then and soil moisture. When observed leaf water falls clearly below the prediction during a water deficit, the date is flagged as possible stress. A rule separates harvest and mowing from stress. The model was tested on fields and a year it had not seen. On 2025 it beat the “same as last time” baseline: R² 0.85 vs 0.75, RMSE 0.081 vs 0.105.
  5. Unusual-month detection. An Isolation Forest compares monthly weather, soil moisture (MERRA-2 and SMAP) and crop indices across all fields and years. For each flagged month, the app compares the month with the same calendar month in other years on that field and names the biggest differences.
  6. Status rules. The verdict combines these signals with simple, transparent rules, so every colour on the map can be explained in one or two sentences.

Benefits

  • Information about the specific field. Weather and soil models describe areas 9–50 km wide. Sentinel-2 at 10 m adds what is happening on this field with this crop.
  • Easy to understand. A colour, a sentence and two or three reasons, instead of raw indices and maps to interpret.
  • Free and scalable. Every input is open data, and a new field needs only its boundary file.
  • Earlier warnings. Farmers can spot an emerging dry spell or stressed crops and decide whether to inspect, irrigate or adjust their plans.
  • Learning from history. The date picker and unusual-month view show how past droughts developed on the farmer’s own fields.

Intended impact

Droughts increasingly threaten crop yields in Wielkopolska. We want farmers to be able to make better water decisions without expensive sensors or technical knowledge. Know Your Field is meant as an early-warning assistant that points to where and when to look more closely. The final decision stays with the farmer, who knows the field best.

Tools and technologies

  • Language: Python.
  • Data processing: pandas, NumPy, xarray, netCDF4, rasterio, Shapely, pyproj.
  • Machine learning: scikit-learn (HistGradientBoostingRegressor for crop stress, Isolation Forest for unusual months). Training ran in Google Colab.
  • Data sources:
    • NASA POWER (MERRA-2 soil moisture, meteorology), NASA SMAP via AppEEARS, NASA SRTM elevation;
    • Copernicus ERA5-Land, ESA Sentinel-2 L2A;
    • FAO GAEZ (explored for crop suitability).
  • Web app: Streamlit, Folium/streamlit-folium (map with Esri satellite basemap), Plotly charts. One shared code base for English and Polish.
  • Hosting and collaboration: GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud.
  • Hardware: standard laptops and free cloud computing; no sensors or special equipment.

What makes it creative

  • Each field is compared with its own past, not with fixed thresholds. “Dry” is relative to the same place and time of year, so the method works anywhere without local calibration.
  • Stress is detected from the gap between expected and observed values. The model learns what a healthy crop should look like after given weather, and a shortfall from that expectation is the warning sign.
  • The app shows its reasons. Every verdict and every unusual month comes with the evidence behind it, so farmers can judge the hint themselves.
  • It combines data at different scales: regional models (9–50 km), 10 m imagery and 30 m terrain. Together they answer three questions: how wet the area is, how much water this crop uses, and whether the plants are already reacting.
  • A time machine. Farmers can replay past seasons on their own fields to calibrate their trust in the tool.

Factors the team considered

  • Honesty about uncertainty. We tested several soil-moisture sources and kept only those we could defend. NISAR radar data, though promising at 200 m resolution, were still at beta stage, covered only a few months and were often fully flagged, so we left them out of this version. SMAP is used only in the unusual-month analysis, because its values over these fields lack NASA’s “recommended quality” flag.
  • Fair evaluation. We tested the stress model on unseen fields and an unseen year and compared it with simple baselines, so its skill is not overstated.
  • Data quality. We filtered cloud, snow, shadows and frozen-soil periods, and did not interpolate across long gaps in the imagery.
  • Usability. Plain language, colours instead of jargon, a bilingual interface, and charts with one-line explanations.
  • The farmer’s role. The app suggests where to look and never gives a diagnosis. As a next step, we plan to let farmers enter their own field observations so the tool can learn from local knowledge.
  • Privacy and security. The app needs no API keys or personal data, and secrets are excluded from the public repository.
